- The paper introduces RAR, a Retrieving And Ranking augmented method for MLLMs (Page 1)
- RAR uses a multi-modal retriever based on CLIP to create and store explicit memory for categories beyond the context window (Page 1)
- During inference, RAR retrieves top-k similar results from memory and uses MLLMs to rank and make final predictions (Page 1)
- The approach significantly boosts accuracy across vision-language recognition tasks (Page 1)
- The method demonstrates a significant improvement on 5 fine-grained visual recognition benchmarks, 11 few-shot image recognition datasets, and 2 object detection datasets under zero-shot recognition (Page 1)
- CLIP excels at recognizing a wide array of candidates but hinders precision in distinguishing subtle differences among fine-grained items (Page 1)
- MLLMs excel at classifying fine-grained categories but their performance declines with an increase in category numbers due to complexity and limited context window size (Page 1)
- CLIP's performance declines on datasets with vast vocabularies or fine-grained categories due to language ambiguity and synonyms (Page 2)
- MLLMs like GPT-4V and LLaVA1.5 are effective for fine-grained classification but fail with extensive vocabularies due to limited context windows (e.g., 2k tokens) (Page 2)
- The proposed RAR method augments MLLMs with external knowledge to improve few-shot/zero-shot abilities on classification and detection datasets (Page 2)
- The core issue is managing large context windows, a critical requirement for accurate processing of vast vocabularies (Page 2)
- The proposed method is named RAR (Retrieving And Ranking) (Page 3)
- RAR uses a multi-modal retriever to retrieve top-k class names and an MLLM to rank them (Page 3)
- The approach achieves a 6.2% average improvement over 11 image classification datasets under the 4-shot setting (Page 3)
- It achieves a 6.4% improvement on the LVIS dataset and a 1.5% gain on the V3Det dataset in zero-shot object recognition (Page 3)
- The method is evaluated on 5 fine-grained visual recognition benchmarks, 11 few-shot image recognition datasets, and 2 object detection datasets with vast vocabularies (e.g., 13204 classes of V3Det [48]) (Page 3)
- CLIP faces challenges in making accurate zero-shot predictions for fine-grained classes (Page 3)
- MLLMs integrate visual images as input tokens alongside text using a vision encoder and bridging mechanism (Page 4)
- MLLMs underperform in tasks requiring vast vocabularies but excel at re-ranking top results from CLIP (Page 4)
- Fine-R [31] uses prompt design for fine-grained perception tasks (Page 4)
- RAG [21] incorporates knowledge from external databases to reduce hallucination and update knowledge (Page 4)
- Previous works use retrieval-augmented approaches with VLMs for long-tailed classification, image-text retrieval, or image generation (Page 4)
- This paper first designs a retrieval-augmented solution for MLLMs (Page 4)
- The research investigates image-image retrieval, image-text retrieval, and an explicit memory component to enhance MLLM capabilities (Page 4)
- Section 3.1 provides background on CLIP, MLLMs, and retrieval-augmentation in LLMs (Page 4)
- Section 3.2 presents the multi-modal retriever module of RAR (Page 4)
- Section 3.3 explains how to apply RAR on downstream tasks via retrieving and ranking (Page 4)
- CLIP combines an image encoder $\varPhi_{\mathrm{img}}$ and a text encoder $\varPhi_{\mathrm{txt}}$ using contrastive learning (Page 4)
- The core mechanism of CLIP maps an input image $\mathcal{I}$ to its most semantically similar category $c \in \mathcal{C}$ using cosine similarity (Page 4)
- Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) such as GPT4V learn to generate predictions over sequences of tokens spanning both image and text modalities (Page 5)
- The MLLM model f, parameterized by weights θ, is conditioned on input sequences x consisting of text tokens x_txt and visual tokens x_img extracted from the input image I via the image encoder Φ_img (Page 5)
- Retrieval-Augmentation introduces a retrieval module R that selects a subset of documents M ⊆ M from an external memory to feed into the LLM θ for generation (Page 5)
- Section 3.2 discusses the multimodal retriever, which queries a large multimodal external memory or database to find relevant information (Page 5)
- The main challenge in multimodal retrieval is efficiently encoding and storing a large volume of images/text embeddings for quick, accurate retrieval (Page 5)
- The CLIP model is used to extract multi-modal embeddings, with the image encoder Φ_img extracting e_img ∈ ℝ^d and the text encoder Φ_text extracting e_text ∈ ℝ^d (Page 5)
- For CLIP ViT-B/16, the feature dimension d = 576 (Page 5)
- In some zero-shot settings, only the text embedding is stored in the memory (Page 5)
- Brute force search is a common method for designing the retriever, requiring iteration over all vectors in the memory M to compute similarity scores (Page 5)
- The efficiency of retrieval diminishes with large datasets, so an index system using the HNSW algorithm is implemented (Page 6)
- Vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$ are transformed into a reduced $\frac{d}{9}$ dimensional space to enhance retrieval speed (Page 6)
- Pre-processing for detection datasets involves cropping based on proposal bounding box coordinates and resizing to a fixed proportion (Page 6)
- A blurring technique is applied to non-target areas to direct MLLMs' focus toward relevant objects in object detection tasks (Page 6)
- The paper describes an inference process using a multimodal retriever and MLLMs for few-shot/zero-shot perception tasks (Page 7)
- For image classification, an image embedding $\hat{e}$ is obtained using a visual encoder $\varPhi_{\mathrm{img}}$ and used to retrieve top-k categories from memory $\mathcal{M}$ (Page 7)
- In object detection, image-to-text retrieval is used because CLIP's feature extraction from small sub-images is limited (Page 7)
- The retrieved category labels and image embedding are sent to MLLMs through a ranking prompt for final prediction (Page 7)
- The proposed method ensures more accurate and contextually aware classification predictions (Page 7)
- The method uses MLLMs to rank retrieved class names based on contextual appropriateness with the input image (Page 8)
- Fine-tuning is performed on a small-scale classification dataset to improve ranking ability and prompt format adherence (Page 8)
- The fine-tuning data consists of approximately 30,000 entries with shuffled category labels to improve the model's ranking ability (Page 8)
- In-context learning is presented as a flexible alternative to fine-tuning (Page 8)
- The paper compares in-context learning (using prompts) to fine-tuning for ranking retrieved results (Page 9)
- Experiments are conducted on fine-grained visual recognition (Bird-200, Cars-196, Dog-120, Flower-102, Pet-37), few-shot image recognition (11 datasets including ImageNet, Caltech101, DTD, SUN397, EuroSAT, RAF-DB, Stanford Cars, FGVC-Aircraft, Oxford Flowers, Food101, Oxford Pets), and zero-shot object recognition (LVIS, V3Det) (Page 9)
- Evaluation metrics include clustering accuracy (cACC) and semantic similarity accuracy (sACC) for fine-grained tasks, top-1 accuracy (%) for few-shot tasks, and AP_r, AP_c, AP_f, AP_all for LVIS, and mAP for V3Det (Page 9)
- A frozen CLIP ViT B/16 model is used as the visual encoder (Page 9)
- The HNSW algorithm is used for retrieval with k=5, except k=4 for the 4-shot few-shot setting (Page 9)
- 30k fine-tuning data is prepared from the FGVC-Aircraft dataset, trained for one epoch with a learning rate of 1e-5 (Page 9)
- The paper evaluates RAR on fine-grained visual recognition using 3 unlabelled images per category to build memory (Page 10)
- Baselines include WordNet+CLIP, BLIP-2, CaSED, and FineR (Page 10)
- RAR achieves the best performance with cACC (58.5%) and sACC (65.3%) (Page 10)
- The text notes that RAR's method optimizes both accuracy and efficiency by first retrieving candidates and then letting MLLMs make predictions (Page 10)
- Section 4.3 introduces the few-shot image recognition setting and mentions CLIP and MLLMs as baselines (Page 10)
- The RAR method boosts top-1 accuracy from 57.0% to 63.2% on the 4-shot setting (Page 11)
- The RAR method boosts top-1 accuracy from 63.0% to 69.8% on the 8-shot setting (Page 11)
- The LLaVA1.5 model fails to make predictions on some datasets due to the limited window size, indicated by '-' (Page 11)
- The RAR method uses the LLaVA1.5 model as the MLLM to rank retrieved results (Page 11)
- The paper introduces Section 4.4, "Zero-Shot Object Recognition," which will present further results (Page 11)
- RAR surpasses CLIP by 19.6 percentage points on APr (rare classes) (Page 12)
- RAR achieves a 1.5 percentage point improvement in APall on V3Det compared to CLIP (Page 12)
- The V3Det dataset contains 13,204 distinct categories (Page 12)
- The retrieval-augmented approach allows MLLMs to effectively navigate fine-grained category landscapes (Page 12)
- RAR uses MLLMs to select correct class names from top retrieved predictions (Page 13)
- The CLIP&K-NN approach provides extensive predictions but may not have the most accurate label as top-1 (Page 13)
- RAR demonstrates remarkable robustness to variations in $k$ (values 3 to 7) (Page 13)
- Based on averaged results, $k = 5$ is selected as the default choice (Page 13)
- RAR is not sensitive to changes in the fine-tuning dataset for ranking (Page 13)

- Fine-tuning significantly boosts the model's ranking capabilities compared to in-context learning (Page 14)
- The results show a consistent improvement in accuracy for fine-tuned models across almost all datasets for both QWen-VL and InternLM-XC2 (Page 14)
- The proposed RAR approach can be seamlessly integrated into various MLLMs for real-world applications (Page 14)
- The method opens up new avenues for research in augmenting MLLM abilities with retrieving-augmented solutions (Page 14)

We first construct a multi-modal retriever that creates and stores multimodal embeddings for visual images and text descriptions. As shown in Fig. 1, upon receiving an input image at the inference stage, our approach retrieves the top- $k$  class names most similar to the image. Subsequently, the MLLMs rank these retrieved candidate results as the final prediction results. To bolster the MLLMs' ranking performance, we explore fine-tuning with ranking format data or in-context learning examples without training. By integrating our retrieval-augmented design, our approach seeks to bridge the gap between the broad generalization capabilities of MLLMs and the need for precise, fine-grained categorization, offering a path forward that preserves the model's extensive knowledge base while significantly boosting its performance on downstream tasks. To evaluate our method's efficacy, we conducted benchmarks in three areas: (1) fine-grained visual recognition across 5 benchmarks, (2) few-shot image recognition across 11 datasets, and (3) zero-shot object recognition on 2 object detection datasets with vast vocabularies (e.g., 13204 classes of V3Det [48]). As presented in the right part of Fig. 1, our findings reveal that our approach notably enhances few-shot learning abilities, yielding an average improvement of  $6.2\%$  over 11 image classification datasets under the 4-shot setting. Furthermore, our method achieves a  $6.4\%$  improvement on the LVIS dataset and a  $1.5\%$  gain on the V3Det dataset in zero-shot object recognition performance. In summary, our key contributions are outlined as follows: (1) We conduct an in-depth analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of VLMs and MLLMs in processing fine-grained datasets. (2) To enhance the fine-grained few-shot and zero-shot perception capabilities of MLLMs, we introduce RAR with a multimodal retriever and the inference pipeline based on retrieving and ranking. (3) Our RAR can be seamlessly integrated into various MLLMs in a plug-and-play manner. 3.3 Inference with Retrieving And Ranking After successfully constructing memory  $\mathcal{M}$  by using our multimodal retriever, our next step is to integrate the memory with the retrieval process and use MLLMs to rank the retrieval results and enhance the performance in few-shot/zero-shot perception tasks. For example, in the inference stage of the few-shot image classification task, we first use the visual encoder  $\varPhi_{\mathrm{img}}$  to process the input image and obtain the corresponding image embedding  $\hat{e}$ . The visual encoder is identical to the encoder used in our multi-modal retriever. The image embedding  $\hat{e}$  is then navigated through the previously constructed memory index and ranked by similarity to identify the top- $k$  related images. Consequently, memory  $\mathcal{M}$  yields the names of the retrieved top- $k$  categories, denoted as  $\{c_1, c_2, c_3, \dots, c_k\}$ . The top- $k$  retrieved results serve as a preliminary filter, narrowing down the vast possibilities to those most likely relevant, based on historical data and the semantic closeness of stored labels to the image content. Since these cropped sub-images are usually small, CLIP's ability to extract features from these low-resolution images is limited. Therefore, in the object detection task, we do not perform image-to-image retrieval but use CLIP's inherent image-text interaction capabilities to conduct image-to-text retrieval. pages.ocr_text: In this appendix, we provide a series of detailed supporting materials to aid in a deeper understanding of our work. Firstly, in Appendix A, we introduce the fourteen image classification datasets involved in our experiments, including seven common datasets and seven fine-grained datasets, as well as two large-scale vocabulary detection datasets. Following that, in Appendix B, we provide detailed information on the prompts used in our RAR, as well as the prompts used in corresponding ablation studies. In Appendix C, we supplement details on the structure and experimental aspects of RAR, dividing the content into three sections: Fine-Grained Visual Recognition, Few-Shot Image Classification, and Zero-Shot Region Recognition. A Dataset Statistics In this section, we delve deeper into the specifics of the fourteen classification and two detection datasets employed in our research. The classification datasets encompass a wide range, from general categories that cover a broad spectrum of common objects to fine-grained types that focus on more specific, detailed distinctions within a particular category. The detection datasets, on the other hand, are extensive, encompassing tens of thousands of object categories. These datasets are designed to challenge the model's ability to identify and categorize objects from a vast array of possible classes. The long-tail nature of these datasets poses a significant challenge for our RAR model. A.1 Classification Datasets In the experimental part, we use a total of fourteen image classification datasets, including seven fine-grained classification datasets and seven common classification datasets. Fine-grained image classification datasets include: Bird-200 [47], Stanford Cars [20], Dog-120 [19], Oxford Flowers [37], Oxford Pets [39], FGVC-Aircraft [34], and Food101 [37]. Common image classification datasets include: ImageNet [7], Caltech101 [11], RAF-DB [25], Sun397 [51], Eurosat [15], DTD [4], and UCF-101 [43]. We present all the utilized datasets in Figure 1. And in Tab. 7, we list the statistics and sources of these datasets in detail. In our fine-grained visual recognition experiments, we employed the following datasets: Bird-200, Stanford Cars, Dog-120, Flowers-102, and Oxford pets. In each dataset, we selected 3 images from the training set to construct our memory and conducted tests on the corresponding validation sets. In our few-shot image classification experiments, we used the FGVC-Aircraft dataset to build fine-tune data and tested our RAR model across eleven classification datasets: Stanford Cars, Flower-102, Oxford Pets, Food101, ImageNet, Caltech101, RAF-DB, Sun397, Eurosat, DTD, and UCF-101. We selected either 4 or 8 images from the training set of each dataset to place into memory, corresponding to 4-shot and 8-shot settings, respectively, and conducted tests across all validation sets.

The car in the image is an Aston Martin, and its styling most closely resembles the Vantage model line. It's a coupe, not a convertible, so coupes have been ranked higher than convertibles. The Audi TTS Coupe, while also a coupe, is from a different manufacturer and thus has distinct styling cues that are less similar to the vehicle in the image. Please play the role of a classification expert, and sort the provided categories from high to low according to the top 5 similarity with the input image. Here are the optional categories: [737-800', '757-300', '767-200', 'A340-300', 'MD-90'] Why did you give this order? The aircraft in the image is a Boeing 757, which is identifiable by its long fuselage, narrow-body, and characteristic nose shape. The -300 series has an extended fuselage compared to other variants, which appears to match the aircraft pictured. The 767-200 and MD-90 have some similarities but differ in specific design elements such as winglets and engine placement. The 737-800 is a shorter aircraft with a different wing design. The A340-300 is a wide-body aircraft with four engines, making it quite distinct from the 757-300. V3Det brings an unprecedented level of diversity to the table. The dataset includes 1,753,000 meticulously annotated bounding boxes, making it an invaluable resource for developing and testing detection algorithms capable of handling a wide variety of object types. Its large number of categories ensures that the dataset has a comprehensive representation of the visual world, making it an ideal testing ground for our Zero-Shot Region Recognition experiments. B Prompt Formats In this section, we delve into the detailed design of our prompts. We have crafted distinct prompts for various tasks to test the capabilities of the baseline model and our RAR model in visual recognition. In our RAR pipeline, the prompt primarily serves to merge the input image with the category information retrieved from memory. It guides MLLMs to rank the retrieved candidate object categories based on similarity. Our prompt format is as follows: Please play the role of a classification expert, and sort the provided categories from high to low according to the {top-k} similarity with the input image. Here are the optional categories:{categories}. Here,  $\{\text{top-k}\}$  is replaced with the number of categories input. And  $\{\text{categories}\}$  is replaced with the top-k categories retrieved from memory.
